extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and practitioners (architects, botanists, naturalists, engineers)
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine-style miscellany of short scientific reports, notices, and practical recommendations covering topics such as acoustical design, plant-light experiments, medical case reports, pedagogy in botany, archaeological and museum news, and an essay competition with submission rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic proportions for music-hall dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most essential requisite to a good music hall or hall for public speaking is that it should be, as to its dimensions, in harmonic proportions. By this is meant that the length, breadth, and height of the room should bear some simple, easily determinable proportions to each other; generally one corresponding with the commensurate ratio borne by the intervals between the tones of the musical scale, which is expressible by the numbers from one to six.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of simple harmonic proportions given: 6:2:8, 6:5:3, 2:5:3, 2:2:4, 2:3:4, or other simple ratios. Design room proportions to follow these simple ratios to improve acoustics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of curved surfaces — avoid circular/elliptical shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Angles, being a disturbing element, may be obviated by adopting curved surfaces, but these must not be circular, for we should then have a whispering gallery, nor elliptical, for then the sounds would be concentrated in the foci; but they should be in the shape of a parabola having its focus very near the contour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When removing angular discontinuities, prefer parabolic contours with the focus near the contour to avoid focused reflections (elliptical) or whispering-gallery effects (circular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating geometry to correspond with sound tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The seats should rise toward the back of the room, to correspond with the tendency of the sound to rise with the ascending currents of air, and to prevent its being caught in the clothing of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design raked seating (rising toward rear) to follow rising sound and reduce sound loss/absorption by audience clothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation design to preserve/direct sound
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of ventilation should be adopted that will rather carry the sound toward the audience than in the other direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ventilation flows so they assist projection toward listeners rather than dispersing sound away from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish material choice based on space per person
rubrics_metrics.description: When the amount of space for each person exceeds one hundred and ninety-five cubic feet, the walls and ceilings should be finished with resonant material; where the amount of space is less than this, the finish should present a repellent, hard, and unsympathetic surface like plaster, or like stone if the space is less than one hundred and fifty feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resonant finishes for very spacious auditoria (>195 cu ft/person). For more confined spaces (<195 cu ft/person) use hard, non-absorbing finishes (plaster); for very small space per person (<150 cu ft/person) prefer stone or similarly hard finishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obstructions from posts and angular gallery recesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The obstructions presented by the supporting-posts and the acute angular recesses of galleries may be avoided by constructing the gallery upon a system of curved iron supports beginning on the floor-line against the wall and rising with a gradual parabolic curve outward, the spaces between which should be filled in with wood or plaster surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curved (parabolic) iron supports rising from floor against wall to outer gallery edge, fill interspaces with wood or plaster to eliminate sightline and acoustic obstructions from posts and angular recesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for party-wall sonority
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Oakey also considers the sonority of party-walls, for which he suggests furring, with lathe and plaster and the removal of the bearings of floor-joists from the walls, as cheap and efficient remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce unwanted transmission or poor sonority in party-walls: add furring, lathe and plaster layers, and avoid floor-joist bearings directly on the wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and format requirements for Red Cross essay competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Committee of the Red Cross has offered prizes for three essays ... The consideration of the subjects must be limited to improvisation, and have no reference to fore-prepared means of assistance. The processes suggested should be illustrated by designs when practicable; and the essays should be full, scientific works, not manuals, and should describe expedients that have been tried and tested for practicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essays must (a) address improvisation only (not pre-prepared instruments/systems), (b) relate respectively to methods of treatment, means of transportation, and improvisation of an ambulance/field-hospital, (c) include designs where practicable, (d) be full scientific treatises (not mere 'how-to' manuals), (e) describe tested/practicable expedients. Language allowed: English, German, or French. Deadline: before April 1, 1883. Awards: $500 for best essay on each topic (if worthy), $100 to unsuccessful competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design elements illustrated by electric-light-on-plants study
rubrics_metrics.description: M. P. P. Deherain's experiments used a conservatory with plants disposed in four groups receiving different treatments (continuous electric light with no daylight; diffused daylight by day + electric light at night; diluted daylight by day + dark at night; shaded garden-bed by day + electric light at night). He used glass globes to enclose the electric light in subsequent trials and measured evolved gas (carbonic acid decomposition) as an indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plant-light experiments with multiple, clearly-distinguished treatment groups and appropriate controls; compare direct exposure versus enclosed (filtered) light; use quantitative measures (e.g., gas evolution) and observe only directly-exposed parts to infer causality of radiation (e.g., violet rays). Repeat and vary enclosure/filters to isolate spectral effects and evaporation-driven growth mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical method for teaching botany ('new botany')
rubrics_metrics.description: In the new way: 'we study objects before books; a few short talks are given; the pupil is directed and set to thinking, investigating, and experimenting for himself ... Before the first lesson each pupil is furnished or told where to procure some specimen for study ... For the first recitation each is to tell what he has discovered. ... The specimens are not in sight during the recitation. In learning the lesson, books are not used, for, if they are used, no books will contain a quarter of what the pupil may see for himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize object-based, inquiry-driven learning: provide specimens prior to lessons, require pupils to investigate and report discoveries, avoid reliance on books at initial stages, keep specimens hidden during recitation to test observation/understanding, and encourage experimentation and independent thinking.
